abrangendo ciências da saúde como medicina, enfermagem, farmácia, fisioterapia, nutrição,

pergunta:
Uma paciente com 64 anos de idade procura atendimento em farmácia comunitária com relato de quedas da própria altura, principalmente durante a noite, quando se levanta para ir ao banheiro. Relata ser hipertensa e fazer uso dos seguintes medicamentos: enalapril 20 mg pela manhã, furosemida 40 mg a noite, além de 6 gotas de clonazepam 2,5 mg/mL para dormir. Conta também que, recentemente, iniciou tratamento com amitriptilina 75 mg para controle de enxaqueca. Diante do caso, o farmacêutico suspendeu a furosemida e encaminhou carta ao prescritor com descrição do caso, solicitando a reavaliação do uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam, devido à potencialização da sedação, com incoordenação motora e aumento do risco de queda. Orientou a paciente a retornar em 15 dias, trazendo as medidas residenciais de pressão arterial e o acompanhamento da adesão ao tratamento por meio de aplicativo de celular. Considerando o raciocínio clínico e a conduta do farmacêutico nesse caso, assinale a opção correta.

A) O farmacêutico agiu adequadamente ao solicitar reavaliação do prescritor em relação ao uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico realizar acompanhamento clínico da forma descrita, sobretudo no que diz respeito ao controle pressórico.
B) O raciocínio em relação ao risco do uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam está correto; a conduta de contato com o prescritor e seguimento do caso também estão adequados; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico suspender medicamentos prescritos, ainda que a furosemida não seja o diurético de escolha para tratar hipertensão.
C) O farmacêutico deveria ter apenas ajustado o horário da furosemida para o período da manhã, a fim de reduzir os despertares noturnos da paciente por diurese; não é permitido ao farmacêutico enviar carta ao prescritor solicitando reavaliação da prescrição, pois tal atitude é considerada antiética, por invadir a área de atuação de outro profissional.
D) O farmacêutico deveria ter ajustado a amitriptilina e a furosemida para o período da manhã, de forma que não houvesse interação desses medicamentos com o clonazepam, o que dispensaria o contato com o prescritor; o acompanhamento dos valores pressóricos cabe ao médico, sendo uma conduta inadequada do farmacêutico assumir esse controle.
E) O raciocínio do farmacêutico está incorreto quanto ao risco da associação de amitriptilina e clonazepam, uma vez que os mecanismos de ação de tais fármacos são distintos; a conduta de suspensão da furosemida foi adequada, considerando-se o risco de queda durante o despertar noturno, o relato da paciente e, principalmente, o fato de ser idosa.

Responda no formato exato: "Resposta: X" — sem mais texto.

Questão:
Uma paciente com 64 anos de idade procura atendimento em farmácia comunitária com relato de quedas da própria altura, principalmente durante a noite, quando se levanta para ir ao banheiro. Relata ser hipertensa e fazer uso dos seguintes medicamentos: enalapril 20 mg pela manhã, furosemida 40 mg a noite, além de 6 gotas de clonazepam 2,5 mg/mL para dormir. Conta também que, recentemente, iniciou tratamento com amitriptilina 75 mg para controle de enxaqueca. Diante do caso, o farmacêutico suspendeu a furosemida e encaminhou carta ao prescritor com descrição do caso, solicitando a reavaliação do uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam, devido à potencialização da sedação, com incoordenação motora e aumento do risco de queda. Orientou a paciente a retornar em 15 dias, trazendo as medidas residenciais de pressão arterial e o acompanhamento da adesão ao tratamento por meio de aplicativo de celular. Considerando o raciocínio clínico e a conduta do farmacêutico nesse caso, assinale a opção correta.

Alternativas:
A) O farmacêutico agiu adequadamente ao solicitar reavaliação do prescritor em relação ao uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico realizar acompanhamento clínico da forma descrita, sobretudo no que diz respeito ao controle pressórico.
B) O raciocínio em relação ao risco do uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam está correto; a conduta de contato com o prescritor e seguimento do caso também estão adequados; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico suspender medicamentos prescritos, ainda que a furosemida não seja o diurético de escolha para tratar hipertensão.
C) O farmacêutico deveria ter apenas ajustado o horário da furosemida para o período da manhã, a fim de reduzir os despertares noturnos da paciente por diurese; não é permitido ao farmacêutico enviar carta ao prescritor solicitando reavaliação da prescrição, pois tal atitude é considerada antiética, por invadir a área de atuação de outro profissional.
D) O farmacêutico deveria ter ajustado a amitriptilina e a furosemida para o período da manhã, de forma que não houvesse interação desses medicamentos com o clonazepam, o que dispensaria o contato com o prescritor; o acompanhamento dos valores pressóricos cabe ao médico, sendo uma conduta inadequada do farmacêutico assumir esse controle.
E) O raciocínio do farmacêutico está incorreto quanto ao risco da associação de amitriptilina e clonazepam, uma vez que os mecanismos de ação de tais fármacos são distintos; a conduta de suspensão da furosemida foi adequada, considerando-se o risco de queda durante o despertar noturno, o relato da paciente e, principalmente, o fato de ser idosa.

Resposta:

reasoning:
We need to parse the question. It's about a 64-year-old patient seeking community pharmacy care, reports falls of her own height mainly at night when getting up for bathroom. She is hypertaensive? Actually "hipertensa" maybe hypertension? She takes enalapril 20 mg in morning, furosemida 40 mg at night, plus 6 drops clonazepam 2.5 mg/mL for sleep. Also recently started amitriptyline 75 mg for migraine control. The pharmacist suspended furosemida and referred to prescriber with case description, requesting re-evaluation of concomitant use of amitriptyline and clonazepam due to potential sedation, motor coordination issues and increased risk of fall. Oriented patient to return in 15 days, bringing residential pressure arterial measures and adherence monitoring via mobile app.

We must choose correct option (A-E) regarding clinical reasoning and pharmacist's conduct.

Let's analyze each alternative:

Option A: "O farmacêutico agiu adequadamente ao solicitar reavaliação do prescritor em relação ao uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico realizar acompanhamento clínico da forma descrita, sobretudo no que diz respeito ao controle pressórico."

Translation: The pharmacist acted appropriately by requesting re-evaluation from prescriber regarding concomitant use of amitriptyline and clonazepam; however, it is prohibited for the pharmacist to perform clinical follow-up as described, especially concerning blood pressure control.

Option B: "O raciocínio em relação ao risco do uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam está correto; a conduta de contato com o prescritor e seguimento do caso também estão adequados; no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico suspender medicamentos prescritos, ainda que a furosemida não seja o diurético de escolha para tratar hipertensão."

Translation: The reasoning about risk of concomitant use is correct; contacting prescriber and following case are adequate; however, it is forbidden for pharmacist to suspend prescribed medications, even though furosemida may not be first-line for hypertension.

Option C: "O farmacêutico deveria ter apenas ajustado o horário da furosemida para o período da manhã, a fim de reduzir os despertares noturnos da paciente por diurese; não é permitido ao farmacêutico enviar carta ao prescritor solicitando reavaliação da prescrição, pois tal atitude é considerada antiética, por invadir a área de atuação de outro profissional."

Translation: Pharmacist should have only adjusted furosemida timing to morning to reduce nocturnal awakenings; sending letter to prescriber is not allowed as it invades other professional's area.

Option D: "O farmacêutico deveria ter ajustado a amitriptilina e a furosemida para o período da manhã, de forma que não houvesse interação desses medicamentos com o clonazepam, o que dispensaria o contato com o prescritor; o acompanhamento dos valores pressóricos cabe ao médico, sendo uma conduta inadequada do farmacêutico assumir esse controle."

Translation: Pharmacist should have adjusted amitriptyline and furosemida to morning so no interaction with clonazepam, dispensing need to contact prescriber; monitoring BP values belongs to doctor, thus pharmacist's involvement is inadequate.

Option E: "O raciocínio do farmacêutico está incorreto quanto ao risco da associação de amitriptilina e clonazepam, uma vez que os mecanismos de ação de tais fármacos são distintos; a conduta de suspensão da furosemida foi adequada, considerando-se o risco de queda durante o despertar noturno, o relato da paciente e, principalmente, o fato de ser idosa."

Translation: The pharmacist's reasoning about risk of association between amitriptyline and clonazepam is incorrect because mechanisms of action are distinct; suspension of furosemida was appropriate considering fall risk during night waking, patient report and being elderly.

We need to decide which is correct based on clinical knowledge and typical ENADE expectations.

First, understand drug interactions: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), used for depression, anxiety, migraine prophylaxis. Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine used for insomnia/sleep. Both can cause sedation, dizziness, ataxia, increased fall risk. Combining them increases sedation and motor impairment. So there is a risk of enhanced sedation and coordination problems. So the pharmacist's request for re-evaluation of concomitant use seems reasonable.

Furosemida is a loop diuretic. Usually for hypertension, first-line might be thiazide or ACE inhibitors, but loop diuretics also used for edema. However, using furosemida at night could cause nocturia, leading to awakenings, possibly causing falls. But the main issue here is that she already has high blood pressure (hypertaens). She is on enalapril (ACE inhibitor) in morning, and furosemida at night. Suspension of furosemida might be considered if it causes excessive diuresis, electrolyte disturbances, or nocturia leading to falls. But the pharmacist's decision to suspend furosemida and refer to prescriber for re-evaluation of amitriptyline and clonazepam is plausible.

Now evaluate options:

Option A says: Pharmacist acted adequately by requesting re-evaluation; but it is prohibited for pharmacist to perform clinical follow-up, especially regarding blood pressure control. Is that true? In many jurisdictions, pharmacists can provide some monitoring but performing full clinical assessment might be beyond scope. However, I'm not sure about prohibition specifically for controlling blood pressure. Typically, pharmacists cannot diagnose or manage hypertension directly; they can advise but not replace medical management. Option A mentions "controle pressórico" - blood pressure control. That sounds like something doctors handle. Could be false.

Option B: Says reasoning about risk is correct; contacting prescriber and following case are adequate; however, it is forbidden to suspend prescribed meds, even though furosemida isn't first line for hypertension. This suggests pharmacists cannot suspend prescription drugs. That seems unlikely; pharmacists often help manage medication regimens, may recommend changes, but suspending a drug might be within their role? Not sure. In Brazil, the role of pharmacist includes advising patients, reviewing prescriptions, possibly recommending adjustments, but actual suspension might require prescriber approval. But the statement "é vedado ao farmacêutico suspender medicamentos prescritos" (it is forbidden for pharmacist to suspend prescribed medications) seems too absolute and likely false.

Option C: Suggests pharmacist should only adjust furosemida timing to morning to reduce nocturnal awakenings; sending letter to prescriber is unethical/invading another profession's area. This denies the right to communicate with prescriber. Probably false.

Option D: Says pharmacist should have adjusted amitriptyline and furosemida to morning to avoid interaction with clonazepam, making contact unnecessary; monitoring BP belongs to doctor, thus pharmacist's involvement is inadequate. This seems off: There's no known major interaction between amitriptyline and furosemida; both affect electrolytes, but not necessarily requiring same time. Interaction with clonazepam? Possibly additive sedation. Adjusting timing might help but not necessary. And monitoring BP is indeed physician's job, but pharmacist can still advise. So D seems wrong.

Option E: States that the pharmacist's reasoning about risk of association between amitriptyline and clonazepam is incorrect because mechanisms of action are distinct; suspension of furosemida was appropriate given fall risk during night awakening, patient's age, etc. This claims that the risk of combining these two is not real because they act differently. But we know both are central nervous system depressants: TCA (amitriptyline) is an anticholinergic, affects GABA? Actually amitriptyline is a tricyclic, affects serotonin, norepinephrine, and also anticholinergic effects. Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine enhancing GABA. They both produce sedation and impair coordination. Even if mechanisms differ, combined effect can increase sedation and fall risk. So saying they're distinct and no risk seems inaccurate. Thus E appears wrong.

Thus none seem obviously correct. Let's examine more carefully.

Maybe the key point: The pharmacist suspended furosemida. Why? Because furosemida at night leads to nocturia and possible falls. The reason for re-evaluating amitriptyline and clonazepam is due to sedation and fall risk. The pharmacist's actions: contacted prescriber, requested re-evaluation, gave instructions to return in 15 days, arranged home pressure measurements and adherence tracking via app. All these seem appropriate. Option A says: "agiu adequadamente ao solicitar reavaliação... no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico realizar acompanhamento clínico da forma descrita, sobretudo no que diz respeito ao controle pressórico." That second part might be false: There's no prohibition against pharmacist doing clinical follow-up, especially after prescribing? Or perhaps in ENADE context, pharmacists are not supposed to monitor blood pressure clinically. Hard to guess.

Option B: says reasoning about risk is correct; contact and follow-up adequate; but it's forbidden to suspend meds, even though furosemida not first line for HTN. That seems also false.

Option C: says only adjust furosemida timing needed, not send letter. Likely false.

Option D: says should adjust amitriptyline and furosemida to morning to avoid interaction with clonazepam, making contact unnecessary; monitoring BP is doctor's job, thus pharmacist's involvement inadequate. Unlikely.

Option E: says reasoning about risk is incorrect because mechanisms distinct; suspension of furosemida was appropriate. This acknowledges suspension was appropriate, and criticizes reasoning about risk. Which one aligns better?

We need to find the best answer according to typical exam logic. Let's break down each component:

- Patient: 64yo female? male? doesn't matter.
- Symptoms: falls of her own height, mainly at night when rising to go to bathroom. Hypertaens (high blood pressure).
- Medications:
   - Enalapril 20 mg AM (ACEI)
   - Furosemida 40 mg AT NIGHT (loop diuretic)
   - Clonazepam 6 drops 2.5 mg/mL for sleeping (benzodiazepine)
   - Recently started amitriptyline 75 mg for migraine control (TCA).

Potential issues:
1. Polypharmacy: multiple CNS depressants (clonazepam, amitriptyline) increasing sedation, dizziness, ataxia -> higher fall risk.
2. Nighttime diuretic (furosemida) causing nocturia -> awakening -> falls.
3. Hypertension: need to control BP. Using furosemida at night may lower BP further, but also cause volume depletion, maybe hypotension? Not sure.

Pharmacist's actions:
- Suspended furosemida.
- Sent letter to prescriber describing case, asking re-evaluation of concomitant use of amitriptyline and clonazepam due to potential sedation, motor coordination issues, increased fall risk.
- Asked patient to return in 15 days.
- Provided residential pressure measurement and adherence monitoring via mobile app.

The pharmacist's reasoning: risk of combination of amitriptyline and clonazepam (both sedative) leading to increased sedation, incoordination, fall risk. That seems correct.

Now check each option relative to this.

Option A: says pharmacist acted appropriately by requesting re-evaluation; but it's prohibited to perform clinical follow-up, especially regarding blood pressure control. Does any law/protocol forbid pharmacist from doing clinical follow-up? In Brazil, pharmacists can provide health advice, but direct clinical management may be limited. However, they can supervise and coordinate. The phrase "controle pressórico" (blood pressure control) might refer to adjusting dosage or monitoring. I doubt it's strictly prohibited. So A likely false.

Option B: says reasoning about risk is correct; contact and follow-up adequate; but it's forbidden to suspend meds, even though furosemida not first line for hypertension. Again, forbidding suspension seems extreme. So B false.

Option C: says pharmacist should only adjust furosemida timing to morning to reduce nocturnal awakenings; sending letter is unethical. That contradicts typical practice where communication with prescriber is allowed. So false.

Option D: says should adjust amitriptyline and furosemida to morning to avoid interaction with clonazepam, making contact unnecessary; monitoring BP belongs to doctor, thus pharmacist's involvement inadequate. This seems overly restrictive and unrealistic. False.

Option E: says pharmacist's reasoning about risk of association between amitriptyline and clonazepam is incorrect because mechanisms are distinct; suspension of furosemida was appropriate, considering fall risk during night awakening, patient's age, etc. This matches our view: The risk of combining amitriptyline and clonazepam is real due to additive sedation, despite different mechanisms. So stating it's incorrect would be wrong. Wait, let's read again: Option E states: "O raciocínio do farmacêutico está incorreto quanto ao risco da associação de amitriptilina e clonazepam, uma vez que os mecanismos de ação de tais fármacos são distintos; a conduta de suspensão da furosemida foi adequada, considerando-se o risco de queda durante o despertar noturno, o relato da paciente e, principalmente, o fato de ser idosa."

So Option E says the pharmacist's reasoning about risk is INCORRECT because mechanisms are distinct. That implies the pharmacist thought there was a risk, but actually there isn't. That seems contrary to standard knowledge. Unless there is nuance: Amitriptyline is an antidepressant, used for migraine prophylaxis; clonazepam is for sleep. Their mechanisms: amitriptyline blocks reuptake of serotonin/norepinephrine, also anticholinergic; clonazepam enhances GABA. They do interact? Possibly synergistic sedation. Many guidelines warn about combining SSRIs/SNRIs with benzodiazepines. For TCAs, caution with benzodiazepines due to additive CNS depression. So definitely risk exists. Therefore Option E's claim that reasoning is incorrect is false.

All options appear flawed. Perhaps we misinterpret the phrasing: We need to pick the one that correctly assesses the scenario. Maybe one of them contains a subtle truth while others contain clear errors. Let's dissect each thoroughly.

Option A: 
- Part 1: "O farmacêutico agiu adequadamente ao solicitar reavaliação do prescritor em relação ao uso concomitante de amitriptilina e clonazepam;" => This is true: He/She did ask for re-evaluation. Good.
- Part 2: "no entanto, é vedado ao farmacêutico realizar acompanhamento clínico da forma descrita, sobretudo no que diz respeito ao controle pressórico." => Is it prohibited? I think not exactly. But maybe in ENADE context, pharmacists cannot perform clinical follow-up, especially regarding blood pressure control. However, they can give advice and arrange monitoring. The phrase "realizar acompanhamento clínico" (perform clinical follow-up) might be beyond scope. Yet the question asks: "Considerando o raciocínio clínico e a conduta do farmacêutico nesse caso, assinale a opção correta." So we need to see which option correctly identifies what is appropriate or not.

Option B:
- Reasoning about risk is correct: yes.
- Contact with prescriber and follow-up adequate: yes.
- However, it's forbidden to suspend meds, even though furosemida not first line for hypertension. This is false: Suspending a medication is generally within the pharmacist's authority to advise and possibly suspend under supervision. But is it illegal? Not sure. Might be false.

Option C:
- Should only adjust furosemida timing to morning: Not enough; also need to address amitriptyline and clonazepam. Denying letter to prescriber is false.

Option D:
- Should adjust amitriptyline and furosemida to morning to avoid interaction with clonazepam: No strong evidence. Also says monitoring BP belongs to doctor, thus pharmacist's involvement inadequate. That seems false.

Option E:
- Reasoning about risk is incorrect because mechanisms distinct: false. Suspension of furosemida was appropriate: maybe true. So overall E mixes correct and incorrect statements. Option E says "O raciocínio do farmacêutico está incorreto ... a conduta de suspensão da furosemida foi adequada..." So half correct, half wrong. Need to find the most accurate overall.

Given all four seem partially wrong, maybe one stands out as least wrong or fully correct. Let's re-express each in English:

A: Pharmacist acted appropriately by requesting re-evaluation; however, he/she is prohibited from performing clinical follow-up, especially regarding blood pressure control.

B: The reasoning about risk of concomitant use is correct; contacting prescriber and following case are adequate; however, it is forbidden to suspend prescribed meds, even though furosemida is not the preferred diuretic for hypertension.

C: Pharmacist should have only adjusted furosemida timing to morning to reduce nocturnal awakenings; it is not permitted to send letter to prescriber as it invades another professional's area.

D: Pharmacist should have adjusted amitriptyline and furosemida to morning to avoid interaction with clonazepam, making contact unnecessary; monitoring blood pressure values belongs to the doctor, thus pharmacist's involvement is inadequate.

E: The pharmacist's reasoning about risk of association between amitriptyline and clonazepam is incorrect because their mechanisms of action are distinct; the suspension of furosemida was appropriate, considering fall risk during night awakening, patient's age, etc.

Which is most plausible? Let's examine typical exam style: Usually one option will be entirely correct. Others contain clear false statements. Look for contradictions: Option A mentions prohibition on clinical follow-up for blood pressure control. That seems like a specific rule that might exist: Pharmacists cannot manage hypertension clinically; they can only advise. Option B mentions prohibition on suspending meds. Option C says sending letter is unethical. Option D says monitoring BP is doctor's job, thus pharmacist's involvement inadequate. Option E says reasoning about risk is wrong. Among these, which is less obviously false? Option A's second clause might be arguable. Option B's third clause is clearly false: you can suspend meds, albeit under guidance. Option C's claim about unethical letter is false. Option D's claim about avoiding interaction and making contact unnecessary is questionable. Option E's claim about mechanisms being distinct is false. So maybe A is the least false? Let's weigh.

But we need to recall typical Brazilian regulations: The "Farmácia Comunitária" and "Encare" maybe emphasize that pharmacists can only provide information and counseling, not perform clinical assessments or prescribe changes. However, they can collaborate with prescribers. The phrase "realizar acompanhamento clínico" (conduct clinical follow-up) might be beyond. Also "controle pressórico" (blood pressure control) is typically done by physicians. So A might be correct in pointing out that pharmacist shouldn't do clinical follow-up for BP control. Meanwhile, the rest of A says pharmacist acted appropriately in requesting re-evaluation. That seems plausible. So A might be the intended answer.

Alternatively, maybe the correct answer is E, because it emphasizes that the reasoning about risk is wrong, and suspension of furosemida was appropriate. But does that align with typical teaching? Let's examine the interplay of amitriptyline and clonazepam. Are they contraindicated together? Usually, combining a TCA with a benzodiazepine can increase sedation and risk of falls. Indeed, guidelines suggest caution. So the pharmacist's concern is valid. Option E says it's incorrect. So E is wrong.

Thus A appears more aligned: It affirms the pharmacist's action (request re-evaluation) and notes a limitation (no clinical follow-up for BP control). Option B also says reasoning correct and contact/ follow-up adequate, but adds a false prohibition on suspending meds. Option A only adds a false prohibition about clinical follow-up. Which false is more severe? Hard to say.

Let's search memory: In ENADE questions about pharmacists, they often test understanding of scope: Pharmacists can review prescriptions, advise, but cannot perform clinical examinations or manage chronic diseases. They can also suspend over-the-counter meds? Not sure. But they can advise to stop certain meds. The phrase "suspender medicamentos prescritos" might be permissible if they recommend discontinuation. Means "it is prohibited for the pharmacist to carry out clinical follow-up of the form described, especially regarding blood pressure control." That would make the whole statement false because it claims the pharmacist acted appropriately but also violates a rule. So A is false.

Option B: says everything is adequate except suspension of meds is forbidden. That also false.
